content: Ophthalmia neonatorum is an eye infection in newborns that can result in blindness, particularly when caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae. To prevent neonatal conjunctivitis and potential vision loss, antiseptic or antibiotic medications are administered either topically to the eyes or systemically shortly after birth. The primary objectives of this review were: 1. To evaluate whether any systemic or topical eye medication is more effective than placebo or no prophylaxis in preventing ophthalmia neonatorum. 2. To determine if any specific systemic or topical eye medication is superior to others in preventing this condition. The search for relevant studies included databases such as CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, LILACS, and three trial registries, with the last search conducted on October 4, 2019. References from included studies were also reviewed, and pharmaceutical companies were contacted for additional data. The review included randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials that compared any topical, systemic, or combination medical interventions for preventing ophthalmia neonatorum in newborns against placebo, no prophylaxis, or other interventions. Standard Cochrane methods were used for data collection and analysis. The outcomes assessed included blindness or adverse visual outcomes at 12 months, conjunctivitis at 1 month (categorized by gonococcal (GC), chlamydial (CC), bacterial (BC), any etiology (ACAE), or unknown etiology (CUE)), and adverse effects. A total of 30 trials involving 79,198 neonates were included. Eighteen studies were conducted in high-income countries (e.g., the USA, Europe, Israel, Canada), while 12 were conducted in lowand middle-income countries (e.g., Africa, Iran, China, Indonesia, Mexico). Fifteen of the studies were quasi-randomized, and all studies were judged to have a high risk of bias in at least one domain. Ten studies included a comparison group with no prophylaxis. Across the 30 studies, 14 different prophylactic regimens and 12 different medications were evaluated. Prophylaxis versus no prophylaxis: None of the studies reported data on the primary outcomes of blindness or adverse visual outcomes at any time point. Very low-certainty evidence suggested that prophylaxis might reduce the risk of GC (4/5340 newborns with prophylaxis vs. 5/2889 without prophylaxis) at one month, but the confidence interval was wide (risk ratio (RR) 0.79, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.24 to 2.65; 3 studies). Low-certainty evidence indicated that prophylaxis may have little to no effect on CC (RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.57 to 1.61; 4874 newborns, 2 studies) or BC (RR 0.84, 95% CI 0.37 to 1.93; 3685 newborns, 2 studies). Moderate-certainty evidence suggested that prophylaxis likely reduces the risk of ACAE at one month (RR 0.65, 95% CI 0.54 to 0.78; 9666 newborns, 8 studies assessing tetracycline 1%, erythromycin 0.5%, povidone-iodine 2.5%, silver nitrate 1%, colostrum, and bacitracin-phenacaine ointment). Very low-certainty evidence was available for CUE (RR 1.75, 95% CI 0.37 to 8.28; 330 newborns, 1 study). Regarding adverse effects, very low-certainty evidence suggested no increased risk of nasolacrimal duct obstruction (RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.68 to 1.28; 404 newborns, 1 study of erythromycin 0.5% and silver nitrate 1%) or keratitis (no events reported in a single study of 40 newborns assessing silver nitrate 1%). Prophylaxis versus other prophylaxis: Evidence comparing different interventions did not identify any consistently superior prophylactic agent. However, most of this evidence was of low certainty and limited in scope. Conclusions: There is no evidence to confirm whether prophylaxis for ophthalmia neonatorum prevents serious outcomes such as blindness or adverse visual outcomes. Moderate-certainty evidence suggests that prophylaxis may reduce the incidence of ACAE in newborns, but the evidence for its effects on GC, CC, or BC is less certain. Comparisons between individual interventions did not reveal any consistently superior option, but the available data were limited. A trial comparing tetracycline, povidone-iodine (single administration), and chloramphenicol for GC and CC could provide valuable insights and potentially identify an effective, universally applicable prophylaxis for ophthalmia neonatorum.
